Scardinius acarnanicus, the Trichonida freshwater rudd, exhibits a maximum recorded fork length of 38 centimeters [Li = 38 centimeters] in Lake Trichonida, a value that positions it among the larger-bodied cyprinids within the Greek ichthyofauna. Field surveys indicate that individuals inhabiting the lake's littoral zone attain this ultimate size only after several years of steady somatic growth, a pattern consistent with the relatively high trophic availability in this ancient lake system. The wet weight at birth is remarkably low, with newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weighing just 0.0019 grams [Wwb = 0.0019 grams], a direct consequence of the small egg diameter of approximately 1.54 millimeters from which they emerge. This minimal neonatal mass, typical of species producing numerous pelagic eggs, necessitates a brief endotrophic phase before the larvae must commence exogenous feeding on zooplankton. The rapid transition from reliance on yolk reserves to active foraging is a critical bottleneck for larval survival in the wild.

Puberty in Scardinius acarnanicus is attained at a fork length of 16 centimeters [Lp = 16 centimeters], a size threshold that marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the production of viable gametes. At this point, the wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 43.7 grams [Wwp = 43.7 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic investment required before reproductive competence is achieved. This size at maturation aligns well with the species' iteroparous life-history strategy, wherein individuals delay first reproduction until a sufficiently large body size buffers the energetic costs of gamete production. The corresponding length-based maturation schedule is intermediate among Balkan leuciscids, balancing the trade-off between early reproduction and continued somatic growth toward the ultimate size. Gonadal development proceeds rapidly once the 16-centimeter threshold is crossed, with vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males becoming histologically evident within the same growing season.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the maximum lifespan of Scardinius acarnanicus extends to approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years], a duration that ranks it as moderately long-lived within the Cyprinidae. This longevity estimate, derived from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith annuli counts, underscores a life-history pace characterized by delayed senescence and sustained reproductive output over many seasons. At this same temperature, the maximum reproductive rate of this species is notable for its magnitude. Gravid females deposit large numbers of adhesive eggs in multiple spawning bouts across the spring and early summer. A single female may release approximately 356 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 356 eggs per day], combining to produce a substantial annual fecundity under favorable thermal regimes.

The ultimate wet weight of Scardinius acarnanicus has been recorded at 661 grams [Wwi = 661 grams] for the largest individuals sampled, a mass that corresponds closely to the maximum fork length of 38 centimeters through a length-weight relationship typical of deep-bodied cyprinids. This asymptotic body mass is substantially greater than that observed in most sympatric leuciscids, reflecting the species' access to abundant benthic macroinvertebrates and plant matter in the productive littoral habitats of Lake Trichonida. The pronounced body depth characteristic of adults contributes to this elevated mass, conferring increased fecundity but also greater vulnerability to piscivorous birds. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Scardinius erythrophthalmus reveal that the Trichonida rudd achieves a higher ultimate body mass relative to its length, suggesting a lineage-specific adaptation to the eutrophic conditions of its endemic lacustrine environment.

Recruitment success in natural populations of Scardinius acarnanicus appears tightly coupled to the spring thermal regime. Adult fish congregate in shallow, vegetated spawning grounds where water temperatures approach 22 °C, the thermal optimum for egg development and larval emergence. The combination of a moderate maximum lifespan of 11 years [am = 11 years] and early maturation at a size of 16 centimeters [Lp = 16 centimeters] fork length confers a life history that is resilient to interannual variation in reproductive success at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. Despite the small wet weight at birth of 0.0019 grams [Wwb = 0.0019 grams], fast larval growth rates permit survival through the vulnerable first growing season. The species' ability to allocate resources toward both somatic growth and repeated spawning events over its extended lifespan underpins its status as the dominant cyprinid in its restricted endemic range.
